title: OET Listening Practice Test 2
instructions: OET Listening has three parts. Part A: Consultation Extracts (note-taking style). Part B: Short Workplace Extracts (main point identification). Part C: Presentation Extracts (detailed comprehension). Listen carefully and choose the best answer.

parts.title: Part A — Consultation Extracts
parts.description: Two consultation extracts. Complete the clinical notes with the information you hear.

parts.title: Part B — Workplace Extracts
parts.description: Short workplace extracts; one multiple-choice question each.

parts.title: Part C — Presentation Extracts
parts.description: Presentation and interview extracts; detailed comprehension of opinion and argument.

listeningScripts.title: Physiotherapy Consultation - Knee Injury
listeningScripts.text:
Physiotherapist: Right, let's assess your knee. Can you walk to the wall for me? Tell me where the pain is exactly. Patient: It's here on the side, below the kneecap. It started last Tuesday when I twisted it playing football. I've been limping since then. Physiotherapist: And have you noticed any swelling? Patient: Yes, quite a bit of swelling, especially in the morning. I've been icing it. Good, that's the right thing to do. Physio: Any clicking or giving way? Patient: No clicking, but the knee did feel unstable when I tried to go up stairs yesterday. Physio: I suspect you may have a ligament strain, possibly to the medial collateral ligament. I'll need to do some special tests. Can you lie on the couch? I'm going to test the stability... yes, there's some laxity there. I'd recommend rest, ice, compression, and elevation for the first week. Take paracetamol for pain. Avoid weight-bearing activities for now. After a week, we can start gentle exercises. I want to see you twice a week for four weeks. If it doesn't improve, we may need an MRI scan. Return to football gradually after six weeks minimum if you progress well. Do you have any questions?

Nurse: Hello Marcus, I'm the mental health nurse from the community team. Your GP referred you because you mentioned feeling low. How long have you been feeling this way? Patient: I'd say about three months now. Ever since I lost my job. Nurse: That must be very difficult. Have you had any previous episodes of depression? Patient: Yes, about ten years ago, but I recovered well with medication and counselling. Nurse: Good to know. Tell me about your sleep and appetite. Patient: My sleep is terrible—I wake at 3 AM and can't get back to sleep. I've lost interest in food, and I've probably lost about 8 kilos. Nurse: Have you had any thoughts of harming yourself? Patient: No, nothing like that. I just feel hopeless sometimes. Nurse: Do you have support at home? Patient: My wife has been very supportive, and we have two children. But I worry about being a burden. Nurse: That's a common feeling with depression. I'd like to refer you back to the psychiatrist for medication review, and I'll arrange weekly counselling for you. We can also discuss a structured return-to-work plan. Employment is important for recovery. Do you think you'd be willing to engage with that? Patient: Yes, I'd like to try. Nurse: Excellent. I'll arrange the psychiatry appointment and counselling to start within two weeks.

Dentist: Mr Sato, we've reviewed the X-rays. Your lower right molar is severely decayed, and the root canal treatment we attempted last month hasn't been successful. The infection has spread to the root tip. I'm recommending extraction. Patient: Oh no. Can't you do another root canal? Dentist: In theory, we could try, but the success rate would be very low—perhaps 20 percent. Extraction is the most reliable option. The tooth is non-vital anyway, so you won't feel pain after extraction. We can discuss replacement options after the extraction site has healed—that takes about three to four months. Then we can consider a bridge, an implant, or a removable partial denture. Patient: How painful is the extraction? Dentist: With proper local anaesthetic, you shouldn't feel pain, just pressure and vibration. Some discomfort afterwards is normal. I'll prescribe antibiotics to prevent infection and paracetamol for pain. Avoid hot foods and drinks for a few days and don't rinse vigorously. Patient: When could you do it? Dentist: We have an appointment next Thursday at 10 AM if that suits you. It should take about 30 minutes. I'll give you written post-operative instructions.

listeningScripts.title: Staff Meeting - New Infection Control Protocol
listeningScripts.text:
Manager: Team, we need to implement new infection control procedures following the recent outbreak. Effective immediately, all staff must wear FFP2 masks when entering patient rooms, regardless of the patient's diagnosis. Hand hygiene is to be performed before and after every patient contact. We're introducing new dispensers on each ward, so please use them. Non-essential visitors should be restricted, and if they do visit, they must wear a mask. We've also arranged mandatory training—it's compulsory and must be completed by the end of this month. There will be spot audits to check compliance. Any breaches will be addressed through our disciplinary procedures. We'll review these measures in six weeks. Questions?

Nurse A: Hi, this is Nurse Sarah from the surgical ward. I'm calling about a patient, Robert Thompson, who's ready for discharge. But he lives alone, and we're concerned about his mobility post-operatively. Can the community team pick him up? Nurse B: Let me check. What's his postcode? Nurse A: It's CH2 5QR. Nurse B: Yes, that's in our catchment area. What is he recovering from? Nurse A: He had a total hip replacement five days ago. He's weight-bearing with crutches and can manage stairs if he takes his time. He'll need daily physiotherapy for the first two weeks and district nursing for wound care. Nurse B: OK, I'll arrange a home visit this week to assess his home for safety, and we'll get physiotherapy scheduled. How long is he staying? Nurse A: We'd like to discharge him tomorrow. Nurse B: That's quite quick—only five days post-op. Can he manage at home? Nurse A: He's keen to go, and his daughter is visiting daily to help with shopping and cooking. We think it's appropriate given his progress. Nurse B: Fair enough. I'll fast-track the home visit. He should expect a call from our team by end of business today to confirm.

listeningScripts.title: Presentation - Vaccination Programme Rollout
listeningScripts.text: Speaker: Thank you all for joining. Today I'm discussing our new vaccination programme rollout for immunosuppressed populations. Background: in recent years, we've seen resurgence of vaccine-preventable diseases in immunocompromised individuals. These patients—those with HIV, on immunosuppressive therapy, post-chemotherapy—often don't mount adequate immune responses to standard vaccines. Our programme aims to identify these patients and provide tailored vaccination schedules. The key innovation is a pre-vaccination assessment that measures baseline immunity levels. Based on CD4 counts and other markers, we tailor the vaccine type and timing. Some patients receive inactivated vaccines, others require live vaccines only after immune recovery. The programme involves general practice, hospital outpatients, and community pharmacies coordinating care. We're training staff across all settings to recognise at-risk patients and refer appropriately. Initial pilot data from three practices showed 95 percent identification of eligible patients and 80 percent uptake. This is significantly higher than historical rates of 30 to 40 percent. The barriers we identified—lack of awareness, inconvenient appointment scheduling, and patient fears about vaccine safety—we've addressed through education and flexible clinic times. Roll-out begins next month across all practices in the region. We expect significant reduction in vaccine-preventable disease burden.
